# PREFACE.

"The further I advance in my studies," wrote Descartes <note>René Descartes (1596–1650) was a foundational French philosopher and mathematician often called the father of modern Western philosophy.</note>, from the college of La Flèche <note>The Royal Jesuit College of La Flèche was one of the most prestigious schools in 17th-century Europe, known for its rigorous curriculum.</note>, the most learned of schools then in existence in Europe, "the more I discover my ignorance. I see clearly, through the reading of books and the lessons of my teachers, that philosophy has always been cultivated by the most excellent minds that have appeared in the world, and yet I find nothing therein that is not still under dispute, and which consequently is not doubtful." And in another letter, he expresses himself as follows: "When I consider the diversity of opinions held by learned persons regarding the same matter, though there can never be more than one that is true, I accustom myself to regard as false everything that is merely probable <term>vraisemblable: This refers to things that appear to be true or likely, but lack the absolute, mathematical certainty Descartes sought.</term>." And when it is with this spirit of wisdom and doubt—or rather, if I may express it so, with this innate instinct for truth—that we see this great philosopher, after having devoted himself to mathematics (the only one of the human sciences where, he said, there was no room for dispute), arrive at the certainty of the existence of God, and likewise at that of the incorporeal essence, the principle

# INTRODUCTION

## TO THE SECOND EDITION OF 1809.

---

The experiments of M. Pététin, a doctor of medicine in Lyon, on <term>cataleptic</term> <note>cataleptic: Referring to catalepsy, a physical state associated with trances or nervous disorders where a person's body becomes rigid and they seem unresponsive to the outside world.</note> women—which have just been published in a volume titled: *On Animal Electricity* <note>original: "De l'Electricité animale"</note>—are the reason that has prompted me to reprint these Memoirs. It is by comparing and bringing together the facts reported in both works that we will be able to more soundly appreciate them and judge the nature of their causes. Facts so similar in many respects must necessarily lend each other mutual support; and while I believe in the <term>intuitive vision</term> <note>intuitive vision: Also known as "clairvoyance" or "transposition of the senses," this was the claim that patients in a deep magnetic sleep could "see" or perceive things without using their eyes, sometimes described as seeing through the pit of the stomach.</note> of M. Pététin's cataleptic women, for the reason that I have many times seen this same vision manifest in many other illnesses subjected to <term>electro-magnetic action</term> <note>electro-magnetic action: At this time, practitioners often linked "animal magnetism" to the newly discovered principles of electricity and physical magnetism, believing a similar invisible fluid governed the human nervous system.</note>; similarly, it seems to me that physicians, on the

faith of their colleague’s observations, should no longer and can no longer doubt today the veracity of my reports and my experiments.

Pététin, or whether it serves only to confirm them, *the possibility, in certain cases, of the development of an intuitive and instinctive faculty in man* <note>intuitive and instinctive faculty: The author is referring to what we might now call "extrasensory perception" or "heightened intuition," which early mesmerists believed emerged when a patient entered a deep magnetic trance.</note>, should and can no longer be a question today. It is not only the <term>magnetizers</term> <note>magnetizers: Practitioners of animal magnetism (mesmerism) who believed they could heal or induce trances by manipulating an invisible "magnetic fluid" in the body.</note>, but a man of the craft—a famous physician—who has just decided the matter affirmatively.

Pététin draws from his curious and surprising experiments; my Memoirs will, I hope, further serve as a safeguard against this danger.

## To Mr. *** .

**Sir**,

*I have the honor of sending you all the details and the results of the experiments that I have had the satisfaction of performing at my home by means of animal magnetism <term>Animal Magnetism: Also known as mesmerism, this was a late 18th-century theory suggesting an invisible natural force (fluid) possessed by all living beings could be manipulated for healing purposes.</term>, the knowledge of which we owe to Mr. Mesmer <note>Franz Friedrich Anton Mesmer (1734–1815) was the German physician who first theorized the existence of "animal magnetism."</note>. *Until at least fifty magnetizers <term>Magnetizer: A practitioner, often without formal medical training, who claimed to manipulate the "magnetic fluid" to treat patients.</term> have reached the point of being able to successfully repeat the experiments they cite, one should not expect to persuade reasonable people of good faith, even less the multitude. # FOREWORD.

---

After the disapproval that two learned and respectable bodies <note>Refers to the two commissions appointed by King Louis XVI in 1784—the Royal Commission (including Benjamin Franklin) and the Royal Society of Medicine—both of which produced reports critical of Mesmer.</note> have given to the discovery of Mr. Mesmer; after they have decided that the effects produced by the means he indicated were due only to the imagination of **weak minds**, or to *imitation*, or else to the painful pressure that can be exerted on certain parts of the body, I feel all the momentary **ridicule** that such an important decision must have cast upon me—I, who was one of the first to sign my private conviction regarding the real effects of <term>animal magnetism<note>The theory that an invisible natural fluid in the body could be manipulated by a "magnetizer" to heal illnesses.</note></term>. Either I must be a visionary <note>In this context, a "visionary" refers to someone who is delusional or easily deceived by their own imagination.</note>, which is possible, or these gentlemen are mistaken, which is also very possible.

This case has already been judged. I hear the most indulgent people say: "One can be a very gallant man and still be enthusiastic about a chimera"; I hear my friends truly pitying me for falling into a proven error; and those to whom I am not known, holding me up to ridicule. One must be right to return to everyone’s good graces; for, even supposing that I were mistaken and that I admitted it, the **ridicule** would not be erased, and, for the enjoyment of life, that is the thing I know most to be feared. *"He has made himself look ridiculous,"* in the mouths

# MEMOIRS

### TOWARD

## THE HISTORY AND THE ESTABLISHMENT

## FIRST PART.

# TREATMENT

## FOR A CHEST CONGESTION.
<note>original: "fluxion de poitrine." In the 18th century, this term was commonly used to describe acute respiratory illnesses like pleurisy or pneumonia.</note>

This treatment is the first I ever undertook; I can even say that it is to this case that I owe, if not entirely my belief in the effects of **animal magnetism** <term>animal magnetism: A theory proposed by Franz Mesmer suggesting an invisible natural force possessed by all living beings that could have curative effects through the movement of a "universal fluid."</term>, then certainly the confidence in my own abilities. Chance dictated that the patient of whom I am about to speak fell into my arms, after only five minutes, into the most perfect state of **somnambulism** <term>somnambulism: Within the context of Mesmerism, this was a trance-like "magnetic sleep" where the patient remained conscious and responsive to the practitioner but was supposedly in a state of heightened internal awareness.</term>—one such as I had never seen before. At the time, I wrote two letters on this subject to the Society formed by Mr. Mesmer <note>Referring to the Society of Harmony (Société de l'Harmonie), a group founded in 1783 to study and disseminate Mesmer's magnetic healing techniques.</note>, which I shall recount here. I was excited to the highest degree, and remarkably proud of all my power: I did not imagine then that the cause was so simple; and without a moment of self-reflection, which showed me clearly that I was far from perfection, I would have been tempted—reflecting on all the "supernatural" things I was doing—to believe myself favored by heaven. Since then, I have only become enlightened at the expense of my own vanity; and it will not be without the same sacrifice that all the Academies...

"The solution to this question—namely, whether one can desire evil as strongly as good—has not yet been resolved for me. A dishonest man would therefore be able to penetrate secrets, abuse the trust of his friends, and take revenge on his enemies with impunity. My only response was that I could not solve this problem myself; for it is impossible for me, I said, to desire evil and good at the same time: if I try to inform myself by asking indiscreet questions, my heart necessarily contradicts them, and I can conclude nothing from the answers given to me. ...to a thread inside a goblet. It is not the well-instructed students of Mr. Mesmer <note>original: "M. Mesmer." ### DEAFNESS FOR TEN YEARS.

The man named *Henri-Joseph-Claude Joly*, a citizen of Dormans, nineteen years old, had suffered, at the age of nine, an acute illness with delirium <note>original: "transport." In 18th-century medical terms, a "transport au cerveau" referred to a state of delirium, agitation, or a rush of "humors" to the brain during a high fever.</note>: following this illness, he was left with a rather severe hardness of hearing. He went to study at the college of Louis-le-Grand, in Paris, at the age of eleven: his ailment did not prevent him from continuing his studies until the class of rhetoric <note>original: "rhétorique." This refers to the penultimate year of the traditional French secondary education system, focusing on the art of persuasion and advanced literature.</note>. But then, having become increasingly deaf, he was forced to leave and return home. He had been back from Paris for nearly two years when he came to find me on October 15 of this year, 1784. He remained under my treatment for seven days and left on the eighth entirely cured, and hearing so perfectly that, however low one might speak to him, he imagined that people were still shouting into his ears.

From the second time I touched this patient, he fell asleep, or, to put it more accurately, he fell into the state of somnambulism <term>somnambulism: in the context of animal magnetism, this is "magnetic sleep," a trance-like state believed to allow the body to repair itself or provide the patient with internal insight into their illness</term>: this was Thursday morning, the 14th. After two hours of

One thing that is infinitely satisfying in the use of animal magnetism <term>animal magnetism: the theory that a "vital fluid" flows through the body and can be manipulated by a healer to cure disease</term> is being able, with the help of a patient in a magnetic crisis <note>original: "crise magnétique." In this context, a "crisis" refers to a trance-like state or "lucid somnambulism" where the patient was believed to gain extraordinary insight into their own body.</note>, to have a *sure* INDICATOR, not only of the seat of their own illness, but also of the illnesses of the various individuals who are presented to them.

When one considers this fact in isolation, and without seeking to understand how it is possible, one is tempted to deny it and regard it as a manifest absurdity: for, it will be said, unless one believes in *sorcerers*, one cannot admit such an assertion. No one is further than I from believing in spells and divinations.

But it must be observed that the knowledge of illnesses and the *foresight* of their symptoms and their termination do not stem from anything supernatural in individuals who find themselves in a state of magnetic crisis. It is not by *pre-diction* <note>The author uses the hyphenated "pré-diction" to emphasize the literal meaning of "speaking before" or foretelling an event.</note> that they judge the causes of illnesses so soundly and surely, but quite simply through a sensation that is unique to them. It is only through sensations that we can have ideas: this truth, so constant and well-recognized <note>This reflects the "Sensationalist" philosophy popular in the 18th century (e.g., Condillac), which argued that all human knowledge comes from sensory experience.</note>, cannot be denied by anything; and what happens to individuals in a magnetic crisis comes once again in support of this...

Regarding what he felt himself while in the magnetic state <term>magnetic state: the trance-like condition induced by the magnetizer, often called "somnambulism," during which the patient was thought to possess heightened internal perception</term>, enabling him to so positively affirm his future sufferings and, finally, his cure: "What name would you give to this?" All the extraordinary nature of the predictions made by patients in the magnetic state <term>magnetic state: the trance induced by animal magnetism, a precursor to modern hypnosis</term> thus vanishes when one considers them as the effect of a particular *pre-feeling* <note>original: "pressensation"</note> that is dependent on the state in which they find themselves. To deny the existence of this sensation because one has not experienced it would be to fall into an error similar to that of a person born blind, who would say that the sense of sight does not exist because he cannot form an idea of it.

—ked, for example, that in the **magnetic state** they have the thought and the memory of everything that occupied them in the **natural state**; whereas, in this latter state, they have no memory of anything that occupied them in the **magnetic state**: which confirms (following what I said above) the existence of an additional sensation in this latter state. One can further employ here the comparison of a person born blind whose sight has been restored. By seeing light, he would surely acquire new ideas, of which he could not have had the slightest inkling before his new state; meanwhile, by acquiring one more sense, he would remember perfectly the way in which he existed without the possession of this sense. The only difference—a very large one—that exists in the passage from the **crisis** <term>crisis: the peak of the magnetic treatment, often appearing as a trance, where the patient's "internal sense" was thought to be most active</term> to the **natural state**, is that here the memory of everything one has experienced is totally lost; which would not happen, in my opinion, to the blind man returned to his original state.

### TREATMENT, THROUGH MAGNETISM, OF A SEVERE AND LONG-STANDING ILLNESS.

THE man named *Philippe-Hubert* VIÉLET, a former gamekeeper and schoolmaster at Espiez, near *Chateau-Thierry*, aged thirty-six, had suffered for four years from a chest ailment and a complication of maladies, as the following consultations attest. Once he had returned to his <term>natural state</term> <note>The patient's normal, waking consciousness, as opposed to the "magnetic" or trance state.</note>, I showed him what he had written in order to reassure him a little; but it was a waste of effort.

On Saturday the 20th, his <term>fit</term> <note>Often referred to as a "crisis" in Mesmerism, these were physical or emotional outbursts believed to be necessary for the patient's cure.</note> took hold of him as usual, around eight o'clock, and lasted an hour and a quarter; my brother and I took it into our heads to play music during the time of his attack; a small sign he made to us gave us the certainty that this was giving him pleasure. Having come out of his fit, we saw him stand up again, with his eyes closed and in the <term>magnetic state</term> <note>A deep trance, also called "magnetic sleep" or artificial somnambulism, where the patient often appeared to have heightened perception or the ability to diagnose their own illness.</note>. Having asked him if he had suffered much, he replied to us that as soon as the music had begun, he had fallen asleep and no longer felt any pain. My plan was to question him about his future fate, following the promise he had given me after his first fit. However, I first thought—in order to distract and amuse him—to sing and to play the harp again (which he had told us had done him so much good); but my surprise was very great to see him gradually open his eyes and return to his natural state: so that this time he had entered and left the magnetic state solely through the help of music, without my brother or I having touched him (12) <note>This indicates a significant observation for the practitioners: they achieved a "magnetic" effect without the traditional "passes" (physical gestures or touch) usually required to induce or end a trance.</note>. We lost, by this means, the opportunity to learn more about his condition.

*Question.* What do you feel?
*Response.* I have lost my speech, which I will only recover tomorrow at the first crisis, which will be at eight o'clock in the morning.
*Q.* Will this end well?
*R.* I think that it will go well.
*Q.* Do you fear tomorrow?
*R.* I will have four crises; the fourth will be very strong, but I hope that it will end happily.

## CONCLUSION.

---

If the most numerous proofs and experiments, repeated with consistent success, could ever persuade men of the existence of something new to them, on what occasion have more been gathered than in the Memoirs <note>original: "Mémoires." These were formal reports or case studies presented to scientific bodies or the public.</note> just read, and in others of the same kind! Falsehood, it is true, has only too often adopted the language of truth, and has known all too well how to borrow its means to gain acceptance for errors. It is dreadful to imagine that, in a civilized society <note>original: "société policée." This refers to a society governed by laws, manners, and refined conduct—a hallmark of Enlightenment thought.</note>, one might sometimes find themselves in a position to doubt the veracity of a certificate.

I am well aware that one can be mistaken, and often affirm in good faith what, with more reflection, one would never have adopted; but this evasion <note>original: "faux-fuyant." A loophole or excuse used to dodge a difficult question or responsibility.</note>, the safeguard of the man of integrity <note>original: "l'honnête homme." In the 18th century, this term described a cultivated, moral, and socially responsible gentleman who acted with reason and honor.</note>, still too often does nothing more than lend another weapon to falsehood. Truth, therefore, has truly—

(6) *Page 32.* To form a correct idea of the state of magnetic somnambulism <note>In the context of Mesmerism, magnetic somnambulism refers to a trance-like state or "lucid sleep" induced by a practitioner, during which the patient was believed to gain heightened awareness or healing abilities.</note>, one must compare this state in the animal kingdom to that of the magnet in the mineral kingdom. The phenomena presented by the latter are analogous to those one should obtain from a person in the magnetic state.

Mr. Mesmer has often said to anyone willing to listen that a man in his natural state had poles and an equator, and was naturally magnetized; that the goal of magnetism was to place this *animal magnet* on its pivot, and that one would immediately recognize in man the same phenomena presented by a magnetized iron bar, also on its pivot: experience proves this assertion to the letter.

A man in his natural state can be compared to a compass needle removed from the point where it sits in equilibrium; if you place it flat on a table, it certainly will not cease to be magnetized for that reason; but as long as you do not replace it on its pivot, it will give you no sign of direction.

It is true that the magnet, in whatever circumstances you place it, will always give certain signs of cohesion, attraction, and repulsion with the iron or filings presented to it, whereas man needs (so to speak) to be on his pivot to present these phenomena: furthermore, friendship, attraction to one’s country, sympathy, antipathy, etc., could—

Mineral magnets, as well as artificial electricity, may indeed have some action on living bodies, but it is only ever as stimulants or as accelerators of the natural movement of these bodies. Their effect must only be temporary; rarely useful, and often harmful if they are too strong or applied too frequently. The reason for this is simple: since the mineral magnet has no direct analogy with our system <note>Meaning the biological/vital system of the human body.</note>, it can only cause fleeting emotions without ever communicating its tonic movement <term>tonic movement: in Mesmerism, this refers to the healthy, balanced vibration or flow of the "universal fluid" within the body</term>; from this results, in its application, the same effects and the same danger that I noted must exist in treatment by artificial electricity.

<meta>This page continues the author’s reflections on his "magnetic" treatments, shifting from a specific case study of a woman in a trance to a broader discussion on the ethics and risks of practicing magnetism from a distance.</meta>

( 186 )

important in itself regarding *magnetism*, to give an idea of the POWER one acquires over magnetic beings; one can act upon them FROM A DISTANCE as well as FROM CLOSE BY; but it is always imprudent to use this power, unless one takes all the precautions that prudence can suggest. This past spring, no accident befell a woman who was a league <note>About 2.5 miles or 4 kilometers.</note> away from me, who for four days entered the magnetic state by my COMMAND at the designated hour, at which time a man from her village would arrive at her home to have her touch a wound he had on his leg; I hope I do not need to add that, to act from a distance in this way, one must have established a prior connection <note>original: "communication"; in Mesmeric practice, this refers to the "rapport" or physical/energetic link established between the magnetizer and the patient.</note> with the being one wishes to operate upon, and have their full consent: if one wished to magnetize someone against their will, it would be a dishonest act, and if one were to succeed, magnetism would be intolerable.

Love, tenderness, joy, sadness—all feelings express themselves through words and song; and these two means combined must therefore necessarily please everyone. It is beyond doubt that our nerves are the organs of our sensations. Music, which acts immediately upon the nerves when it is united with the agent of nature <note>The "universal fluid" which Mesmerists believed was the medium for healing energy.</note>, must therefore provide it with a reinforcement that can only be favorable to the beneficial effect one wishes to obtain. This is what happened to Joly, and what perhaps contributed to dividing his nervous crises into a much greater number of periods than he had at first foreseen, and allowed him the strength to endure their duration. One will easily sense the risk this young man would have run if, on Tuesday, instead of four attacks scattered throughout the day, he had experienced them gathered into one; it is to be presumed that he would have succumbed to them, and would have only too well verified his fatal premonitions. This example supports the methods of Mr. Mesmer. The instruments he plays sufficiently prove the aid he felt could be drawn from music, and the choice of his instrument likewise proves his profound reflections. Indeed, the harmonica <note>The glass harmonica, an instrument made of nested glass bowls played with wet fingers, favored by Mesmer for its ethereal, "vibrating" tones.</note> can be considered as a collection of small electrical plates, whose accumulated movement manifests as sound, which, combined with animal motion <term>mouvement animal: the internal flow of vital or magnetic fluid within the living body</term>, must produce a very effective magnetism.

In the absence of Mr. Mesmer, the best means to take to obtain good experiments in Paris would be, I believe, to choose from among his students two prudent and wise men, driven by personal inclination and affection to relieve humanity, and independent enough from surrounding circumstances to be able to devote themselves without reservation to the practice of animal magnetism. Mr. Mesmer said all of this; but what supernatural means would he have needed to control three hundred students, most of whom still doubted his doctrine! My brother, when at my house, was quite willing to be only a conductor, as I have just said; thus he performed the same good and produced the same effects as I did on my patients. If I were at his house, we would reverse roles, and the same results, I hope, would follow.

When he wished to treat the patients at my tub <term>baquet: a large wooden vat filled with water and iron filings, used as a collective battery to concentrate and distribute "magnetic fluid" to patients through metal rods</term>, he would come to inform me; if it suited me, I would touch his thumbs for a few moments. (15) Page 168. Mr. Mesmer says, in one of his propositions, that animal magnetism will present the same phenomena as those observed in electricity. Nothing is more true; attraction, repulsion, communication through the chain <note>The "magnetic chain" was formed by patients holding hands or connected by cords to allow the "universal fluid" to circulate through the group</note>, charging and discharging at will; all these different effects are as easy to produce by animal magnetism as by electricity. As soon as any being is recognized as susceptible to becoming a magnetic somnambulist <term>somnambulisme magnétique: a trance-like state, discovered by Puységur, where the patient appears asleep but can speak, follow commands, and sometimes displays heightened sensitivity</term>, one can boldly challenge the most skeptical people by making them witnesses to these different phenomena. Blindfolding a magnetic subject does not hinder the success of the experiments in any way, and one should never refuse to do so to strengthen the belief of those one wishes to persuade.

Several people have asked me by what sign one can recognize when a patient is in the state of magnetic somnambulism; nothing is easier to notice: first, he must have no rapport <note>original: "analogie"—referring to the specific physical and spiritual connection established between the magnetizer and the subject</note> with anyone other than the person who magnetized him; he must answer and obey only him. The approach of any living being, except for the magnetizer, must be unbearable to him. But if one wishes to conduct an experiment more convincing for oneself and for others, place your magnetic subject in a corner of the room, and even blindfold him, if you wish; he must answer only to you. During the printing of my work, an event occurred which seems to me of a nature to interest you. I will first give you an account of it with the utmost fidelity; after which I will have you observe the consequences resulting from it.

Chance would have it that Victor <note>Victor Race was a young peasant on the Puységur estate whose reaction to magnetism led to the discovery of "artificial somnambulism," a state similar to a deep trance or hypnosis.</note>, the first patient mentioned in these Memoirs, came to Paris to bring one of his brothers there. He came to find me, told me the reason for his trip, and announced that he was leaving the next day. Having questioned him about his health, he informed me that, eight to ten days before his departure from Buzancy <note>Buzancy was the location of the Marquis de Puységur’s estate and the site of his famous "magnetic tree" where he treated local villagers.</note>, he had suffered a violent fall; since then he had been suffering considerably in his head, and that every evening he felt bouts <note>original: "mouvemens"—literally "movements," used here to describe the recurring onset or fluctuations of fever symptoms.</note> of fever. His indisposition prompted me to have him stay, hoping, with the help of magnetism, to be able to cure him promptly.

Thursday morning he heard all the noise from the street.

Finally, at a few minutes before one o'clock, although I was expecting him to wake, I was surprised by the noise I heard; it was Victor, who, like a lightning bolt, leapt from his armchair, and with his eyes wide open, made but a single jump to the window. The greatest astonishment then followed his outburst; and approaching a mirror, he stood stupefied by the length of his beard. I asked him if he did not remember what had happened to him, or his various awakenings where he had found himself trembling. Without the length of his beard, he would never have been able to believe that four days had passed during which he had, so to speak, not lived.

This event will provide you, sir, with several conclusions that you will turn to your personal benefit, and to that of the magnetic science.

You have been able to see by my account that the effect of magnetism is to always act upon a sick individual, or one who carries the impending seed of a disease—an effect which ceases with the restoration of perfect health. This is proven by the example of Victor, who, having remained subject to magnetic action as long as he carried some disorder <note>original: "dérangement." From this we can safely conclude that there is no perfect cure for any subject who remains susceptible to *crises* <note>original: "crise." This refers to "magnetic sleep," a trance state discovered by the Marquis de Puységur where the patient appeared to be asleep yet could speak and follow instructions.</note>, and that the magnetizer <note>term: "magnétiseur." Without this condition, any apparent cure must leave one fearing a relapse or some unfortunate consequences. This observation, already made regarding the cures of Joly and Viélet, gains new strength from that of Victor.

Secondly, Victor's story should serve as a lesson for every magnetizer not to attempt experiments indiscreetly, and without having ensured all possible means to make them succeed and to prove their sincerity.

When you wish to present the phenomena of magnetic somnambulism to someone, take care that the persons to whom you communicate this remarkable experience already have some preliminary notion of somnambulism themselves, so as not to suddenly present their incredulity with a wonder <note>original: "prodige." Referring to the extraordinary or seemingly miraculous nature of the magnetic trance.</note> too difficult to conceive.

With such dispositions, there is no physical experiment <note>original: "expérience physique." It is with a kind of violence and a smile of pity that he ventures to use the machine <note>In the context of Mesmerism, the "machine" usually refers to the *baquet*, a wooden tub filled with water and iron filings designed to concentrate "magnetic fluid."</note> I entrust to him; and his incredulity making him clumsy, he ends up fatiguing the instrument, without gaining any profit from it.

Do not be in a hurry to want to *prove*: magnetism is established today on such a solid foundation that it will prove itself through a series of naturally occurring facts, to the evidence of which minds will yield sooner or later. ## PREFACE.

In physics, a single fact proves more than all possible reasoning; this is, I believe, an axiom <note>An "axiom" is a statement or proposition which is regarded as being established, accepted, or self-evidently true.</note> that no one can contradict. The effects produced by *animal magnetism* <term>animal magnetism: Originally termed "mesmerism," this was the belief in an invisible natural force (a "fluid") that flowed through living beings and could be manipulated for healing.</term> are physical: it is therefore only through a multiplicity of facts and repeated experiments, always with the same success, that one can claim to convince the public of the existence of the agent <note>In 18th-century science, an "agent" referred to a specific force or substance—like electricity or heat—that caused a physical change.</note> being presented to them.

The most appealing *theory* regarding animal magnetism, if it is not supported by facts that verify its truth, will only be received with indifference, or will be regarded as a new system against which one must always remain on guard; for arguments can always be countered by other arguments, and indecision is usually the result of such conflicts of opinion. But what can be opposed to facts which, if they have been carefully observed, can be re-

Truth cannot lose its rights, and confusion is always the lot of those who, through bad faith, refuse to recognize it.

The practice of <term>animal magnetism: An 18th-century medical theory, also known as Mesmerism, which proposed that an invisible natural force or "fluid" in the body could be manipulated to heal illness.</term> is very new; until now, we have only a small number of facts that prove its utility. ## SECOND PART.

---

People have heard too much of the phenomena presented in Paris last winter by the <term>somnambulism: In the context of early magnetism, this refers to a "magnetic sleep" or trance state where the patient was said to be lucid and capable of diagnosing their own illness.</term> of the girl named *Madeleine*, and the opinion formed regarding the singular state of this girl has been too erroneous for me to dispense with providing some details of the facts that so many people witnessed.

My account may well fail to satisfy a biased public; but, once again, I do not pretend in any way to convince them: my sole aim is to converse with those who are as convinced as I am of the existence and properties of <term>animal magnetism: A theory, popular in the late 18th century, positing that an invisible natural force (a "fluid") could be channeled by a practitioner to heal patients.</term>.

<summary>The author introduces the second part of his memoirs by addressing the famous and controversial case of a patient named Madeleine in Paris, intending to clarify the facts for supporters of animal magnetism.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the introduction to the Second Part of the Memoirs, detailing the specific history of the patient Madeleine, who was previously mentioned as a subject of controversy in Paris.</meta>

Madeleine had undergone <term>magnetic treatment: A therapy based on the theories of Franz Mesmer, where a practitioner uses hand gestures (passes) to influence the "universal fluid" within a patient to restore health.</term> at Buzancy last autumn for three weeks: since I had not seen any beneficial change take place in her at that time, and despairing of being able to cure her, I had sent her back to her home village.

I was far from imagining that four months later this girl would serve for public experiments in Paris, since, of all the patients cited in my Memoirs, she was without contradiction the one who presented the least satisfactory phenomena: she had no distinct sensations regarding her own state, no <term>pressensation: A term used in early magnetism to describe a patient's supposed ability to "feel" or predict the future course of their illness.</term>, understood nothing of the illnesses of others, and showed a very limited intelligence during her crises; but considered as an *animal magnet* <note>original: "aimant animal." In the context of early mesmerism, this refers to a person who becomes highly sensitive to the magnetic fluid, acting almost like a physical magnet that responds to the practitioner's influence.</note>, it was impossible to see a more perfect one.

Therefore, after having shared with some of my friends the various events that occurred during my treatments at Buzancy, and several of them wishing to see some effects analogous to those I had cited, I determined to send for this girl, whom, otherwise, I would probably never have thought of again.

My plan was that they would be the only spectators of my experiments, foreseeing well that, despite the opinion I might flatter myself with holding...

Unfortunately, it became known that Mr. *Sæffer*, a physician, had visited my home, and that he admitted to having seen an extraordinary fact of which he could not doubt.

With a hammer, I strike a steel bar at one of its ends; immediately some effect manifests at the opposite end, and the bar becomes magnetized. Therefore, I say again, this is an effect of motion.

What I mean to say here may seem enigmatic to many people, but will be perfectly understood, I hope, by all **magnetizers** <note>Magnetizers were practitioners of "animal magnetism" (Mesmerism), who believed they could heal by channeling a "universal fluid" through their hands or intent.</note> who are somewhat knowledgeable. # TREATMENT
## OF AN INFLAMMATORY FEVER.

---

**A** man named *Denis*, my kitchen boy, had experienced bouts of fever for two or three days when he decided to take *medicine* <note>In the 18th century, "taking medicine" often specifically referred to self-administering a purgative or laxative, a common but sometimes dangerous home remedy.</note> without saying anything to anyone.

On Sunday, March 27, he had the indiscretion <note>Meaning a lack of judgment or care for his own physical state.</note> to perform his work all day; and that evening, overwhelmed by fever and a violent headache, he was forced to take to his bed: the night was stormy. A groom sleeping in the same room as he told me that he had suffered from delirium <note>Original: "le transport"—a term used to describe a state of mental wandering or frantic agitation caused by high fever.</note>: blood had come from his mouth and nose, so much so that his sheets were entirely stained by it.

It was not until the following morning, the 28th, that I learned of his illness: I went to see him immediately and began to magnetize <note>Applying "animal magnetism," the technique developed by Franz Mesmer involving the movement of hands over the body to balance "vital fluids."</note> him. ### CURE FOR STOMACH AILMENTS OF ONE MONTH'S DURATION.

**The** man named *Jean-Hubert Thuillier*, the village schoolmaster, came to find me on the morning of Saturday, May 6, saying he had been suffering from his stomach for eight days, to the point of being unable to work or sing in church.

### TREATMENT OF OBSTRUCTION AND A FIXED DEPOSIT <note>In 18th-century medicine, an "obstruction" referred to a blockage in the body's vessels or organs, while a "deposit" (dépôt) meant a localized accumulation of "morbid humors" or fluids, often appearing as a swelling or internal mass.</note> IN THE BODY, HABITUAL NOSEBLEEDS, VAGUE PAIN IN THE HEAD AND NECK, AND UNIVERSAL WEAKNESS FOR EIGHT YEARS.

THE man named *Henri Caron*, a former postillion <note>A rider who mounted one of the leading horses drawing a carriage or mail coach.</note> of the postal service of Vivrai, aged twenty-nine, from the parish of Baune, near Neuilly-Saint-Front, came on Ascension Day <note>A Christian holiday commemorating the ascent of Jesus into heaven, occurring forty days after Easter.</note> to consult me. ### CONTINUATION OF THE TREATMENT OF CATHERINE MONTENECOURT.

CATHERINE MONTENECOURT had said that it would not be until the spring that she would entirely recover her health: consequently, I admitted her to my treatment on April 20th. She had suffered several colds during the winter which had greatly fatigued her chest; a <term>bloodletting</term> <note>original: "saignée"; a common medical practice of the time involving the withdrawal of blood to cure illness. Many magnetizers, following Franz Mesmer, were critical of this practice, believing it depleted the patient's vital fluids.</note>, which someone had the imprudence to perform on her, had also interfered with the periodic return of her menses; and, during her last cycles, she had experienced quite violent colics.

The ordinary remedies of medicine that are administered in such cases usually only act upon the branches of the plant, sometimes even cutting them down; from which necessarily follows a visible and momentary improvement. Usually, the most apparent symptoms subside, the pains cease, and the patient, fully satisfied at no longer suffering, looks upon his physician as a guardian God <note>Original: "Dieu tutélaire." A reference to a protective deity; here used to show the patient's misplaced or premature gratitude.</note>: but the roots of the plant are still alive; after some time, they bear fruit once more; the branches regrow with all the more vigor because the plant has already been pruned, and the patient finds himself in a worse state than he was in before. It is then necessary to have recourse a second time to the skillful physician who cured him so well the first time. One can imagine that he then requires greater means than the first ones he employed, stronger shears to prune the new shoots full of sap and vigor that have grown back. If he only uses those he used previously, he will bring no relief. But finally, I suppose that the physician has, in addition to his science, much experience <term>experience</term> <note>Original: "expérience." <meta>This page continues the Marquis de Puységur’s argument that conventional medical treatments merely prune the branches of chronic illness rather than pulling up the roots. It follows the thought that a physician might succeed once in providing relief, and then...</meta>

perhaps even a second time in restoring a precarious health to his patient; but beware the third relapse! The third ramification of the plant will be terrible to prune; a greater quantity of branches, a more active vegetation... What can the physician do then? Will he dare to employ means more powerful and more incisive than those he used the second time? He knows all too well that the patient would not withstand them. What is to be done then? Alas! palliatives, giving opium, sending the patient to the waters <note>Original: "envoyer aux eaux." A reference to prescribing visits to thermal springs or spas, a common 18th-century treatment for chronic conditions.</note>, etc... These are the only and final resources which cover, I dare say, not the ignorance of physicians, but most certainly the infancy of medicine today.

A means tending, from the first moment of its application, to destroy the principle of the illness, to attack the plant at its root, is, beyond question, the only effective remedy to employ in chronic illnesses. Animal magnetism <term>animal magnetism</term> <note>Also known as Mesmerism, this theory proposed that an invisible natural force (fluid) possessed by all living things could be channeled by a practitioner to heal the sick.</note>, well administered, is, I believe, one of the most powerful means to achieve this desirable goal. ### AN INTERESTING CURE, DUE TO THE EVENTS IT PRODUCED.

Agnès Remont, the wife of the blacksmith <note>original: "maréchal-ferrant," a farrier or blacksmith who specialized in shoeing horses.</note> of Buzancy, very strong and well-constituted, twenty-four years of age, had been cured this past spring of an obstruction in the body <note>original: "embarras dans le corps." In 18th-century medicine, an "embarras" usually referred to a blockage or congestion of the humors or the digestive tract.</note>, which occurred following a difficult childbirth <note>original: "une couche fâcheuse."</note>. ### MY ILLNESS, AND RELATED DETAILS.

After having had the happiness of restoring so many individuals to life through the help of <term>animal magnetism</term> <note>Also known as Mesmerism, this was the 18th-century theory that an invisible natural fluid or energy flowed through all living things and could be manipulated by a "magnetizer" to heal illnesses.</note>, nothing could better complete my satisfaction than to owe my own health to the same means that I had so blindly and so usefully employed for others.

The account of my illness and my prompt recovery will, I hope, give a new idea of the power of animal magnetism and the new pleasures it has afforded me.

The following day, Tuesday, Viélet was able to confirm the return of my health; and having himself woken up on his own after an hour-long <term>crisis: in the practice of animal magnetism, a "crisis" was a state of trance or convulsion believed to be the point where the body’s "internal sense" identifies and begins to expel illness</term>, he put my mind at ease regarding his own condition, so that on the same day we found ourselves cured at the same time. I was able to enjoy, with a pleasure that cannot be described, the sweet satisfaction of owing my health—and perhaps my life—to the very same man who had received his from me. The memory of Viélet’s action will always remain present in my mind; I believe it will never be possible for me to be unhappy while thinking of it. Could I have been better rewarded for all the care I had given him! Oh, how good the heart of man is! J.-J. Rousseau <note>Jean-Jacques Rousseau (1712–1778), the Genevan philosopher whose ideas on the innate goodness of humanity and the corrupting influence of society deeply resonated with Puységur’s observations of patients in magnetic trances.</note>, the man whose habitual state perhaps most closely approached the state of a magnetic crisis, used to repeat incessantly to his friends who wished to reconcile him with humanity, from which he always withdrew: *Man is good*, he would say, *but men are wicked*.

It is even likely that I would never have spoken of magnetism in this city, had the unforeseen event of the illness of the young Count *Louis de Rieux* not fixed everyone's attention on the subject.

Count Louis de Rieux had felt, on the evening of the 24th, chills and feverish movements; on the evening of the 25th, he felt the same discomforts, to which were added quite sharp pains in the shoulder and in the neck: when he breathed a little deeply, the pains were more acute. Glass, according to its electrical properties, is, as we have said, an excellent conductor of **animal magnetism** <term>animal magnetism: the theory that an invisible natural force or "fluid" flows through living beings and can be manipulated to heal diseases</term>. ### *Deposition of the man named Dupré, a soldier of the Hesse-Darmstadt regiment, in Houdouard’s company, to Mr. de Puységur, in the presence of the undersigned.*

> “The cause of my illness comes from the sorrow of seeing myself as strictly restrained <note>original: "court tenu"; this suggests Dupré felt stifled or oppressed by the rigid discipline of military life</note> as I am at the barracks, and of not being liked by my comrades. A week from next Saturday, I will need to be purged, and I will no longer fall into a crisis <term>crisis: in the practice of animal magnetism, the "crisis" was a violent physical reaction or fit believed to be the moment when the body expelled the cause of a disease</term>.

A week from Friday, the crises will end for me, and I will not fall back into them the following Saturday.”

## CONCLUSION.

---

I have presented, I believe, in the course of these <term>Memoirs</term> <note>original: "Mémoires." This refers to Puységur’s published collection of case studies and observations on magnetic sleep.</note> and in those preceding them, more facts than are necessary to persuade those who read them of the existence of *animal magnetism*, and of its utility in the treatment of most illnesses.

Anyone who wishes to carefully examine the various details of the <term>cures</term> <note>original: "cures." In this era, the word referred both to the process of treatment and the successful recovery itself.</note> described therein will not be able, I believe, to help but recognize the truth of the facts reported; and by granting them the credit they deserve, will be forced to agree that this new means of healing is infinitely simpler and more accessible to all people than any known to this day.

I have, furthermore, endeavored to persuade all people that they possess within themselves the faculty to magnetize, and that the efficacy of magnetic treatments is in proportion to *perseverance*, to...

<summary>The Marquis de Puységur begins his concluding remarks, arguing that his recorded case studies provide sufficient proof for the reality and medical benefits of animal magnetism. He asserts that the ability to heal through magnetism is a natural human faculty that is simpler and more accessible than traditional medical practices.</summary>
<keywords>animal magnetism, medical proof, universal healing, Marquis de Puységur, perseverance, memoirs</keywords>

--- Page 464 ---
<meta>This page continues the Marquis de Puységur’s concluding arguments from the previous page. He finishes his sentence regarding the qualities necessary for successful magnetism—perseverance, sensitivity, and good will—before moving into a philosophical reflection on healing as a natural human instinct that has been lost to modern "science."</meta>

( 428 )

*sensitivity*, and the *good will* of the <term>magnetizers</term> <note>original: "magnétiseurs." These were practitioners who believed they could direct a "universal fluid" to heal others.</note>.

Every human being, as they grow, acquires the faculty to heal their fellow man, just as they acquire the faculty to reproduce. These two faculties are the results of <term>compassion</term> <note>original: "commisération." Puységur links the physical act of healing to the emotional capacity for pity and shared suffering.</note> and love, two sentiments as compelling as one another, and certainly common to all people.

Nothing proves better how far we have strayed from the <term>laws of nature</term> <note>original: "lois de la nature." A central idea in 18th-century thought, suggesting that humanity is happiest and healthiest when following natural instincts rather than artificial social constructs.</note> than this total abandonment of one of our most important faculties (19).

There certainly existed in the past societies in which <term>animal magnetism</term> <note>original: "magnétisme animal." The theory that an invisible natural force exists in all living things and can be used for healing.</note>, this medicine so easy and so natural, was practiced; but in the simplicity of <term>ancient customs</term> <note>original: "mœurs anciennes."</note>, it must have been enough for people to let themselves be moved by the impulse of their compassionate souls to bring about prompt and certain relief. The <term>art of healing</term> <note>original: "art de guérir."</note>, far from being a *science*, was, so to speak, a need; thus, no more rules were required for this operation than for all physical actions of primary necessity that we perform without calculation.

If one supposes, in effect, that there existed a society of just and good men, satisfied in...

(5) *Page 274.* I am not of the opinion of several people practicing magnetism who believe that there are different means of charging oneself with electricity to act more strongly on a patient; I, at least, know of no means for this, and I have never believed I should seek any.

A magnetizer does not deplete his *vital principle* <term>Vital principle: A hypothetical force or "spark" once thought to distinguish living things from non-living matter; often associated with Mesmer's "animal magnetism."</term> when he magnetizes; he may tire his faculties <note>Original: "ressorts," literally "springs." One could compare the magnetic operation to that of a candle whose flame can light twenty others without losing anything of its incandescence. An inflamed body does nothing other than direct its action upon another body in which the *phlogiston* <term>Phlogiston: An obsolete scientific concept of a fire-like element contained within combustible bodies. (6) Page 276. The ancients held the idea of two essences in man, one spiritual and the other material.

The ancient theology of the Hebrews spoke of man according to these three relationships: *mind, soul, and body* <note>Original Latin: "mens, anima et corpus."</note>. The Egyptians likewise believed man to be divided into three distinct parts: into understanding, into soul, and into a terrestrial and mortal body. They regarded the understanding as the spiritual part of the soul; the soul as the subtle and delicate body in which the understanding was clothed; and the terrestrial body as animated by the soul—that is to say, by the subtle body <term>Subtle body: In ancient philosophy, a "quasi-material" substance, finer than visible matter, that was thought to act as a bridge between the physical body and the immaterial spirit.</term>.

Pythagoras, who had drawn much enlightenment from the Egyptians, taught that the intelligent soul was clothed in a subtle body that he called the *chariot of the soul* <note>The "chariot of the soul" (or *okhema*) is a concept from Neoplatonism and Pythagorean thought, describing the vehicle by which the soul descends into the physical world.</note>, which served as the communication between the two natures. He claimed that this intermediary was luminous, and that, moved by the intelligent soul, its action could extend over all of nature. This *chariot of the soul*, this luminous intermediary of Pythagoras, bears a great resemblance, it seems to me, to what we designate today under the name of *magnetism* or *animal electricity* <term>Animal electricity: Also known as Mesmerism; the belief that a natural invisible force (fluid) possessed by all living things could be channeled for healing.</term>; and I doubt that the Greek philosopher could have explained himself more clearly had he known the new phenomena that this discovery presents to us.

Pythagoras saw only man as endowed with an intelligent and immaterial soul, and judged that the sensitive soul—or the principle of sensations and instinct in animals—must be of the same nature as the animal soul or the subtle chariot of the human soul. These

(8) *Page 285.* To calm an effect that is too violent produced by magnetism, it is once again in the **will** <note>A central tenet of the Marquis de Puységur’s school of magnetism was that the practitioner’s mental intention, or "will," was the primary force, rather than physical fluid or magnets alone.</note> alone that one must seek the power. When I magnetize a patient, I never know in advance the effect I am going to produce; but what I am quite sure of is that my magnetic action must be useful and beneficial to them. Having no reason to prefer one effect over another, the sensation of pleasure or pain that I experience is the only rule of my conduct. If I see, for example, that my magnetic action occasions the onset of **spasms**, **delirium**, **convulsions**, etc., these effects certainly displease and distress me, for the reason that my goal being to remove or calm the ailments of a patient, I cannot take pleasure in seeing them suffer new ones: then, quite mechanically, the will I have to make the violent effect I have produced cease softens my **touch** <note>Refers to the physical contact or "magnetic passes"—hand movements made near or on the patient’s body to direct the supposed fluid.</note> and diminishes my action.

(13) *Page 352.* Magnetic somnambulists <term>Magnetic somnambulists: individuals placed into a deep trance-like state via animal magnetism (Mesmerism), believed to possess heightened sensory or diagnostic abilities.</term> should not always be assumed capable of knowing the illnesses of others: this ability, being merely a sensation in them, weakens or improves depending on the different states in which they find themselves. All those whom I have used as *physicians* <note>original: "médecins." In the context of early 19th-century magnetism, patients in a trance were often consulted as "physicians" to diagnose themselves or others.</note> have experienced this fluctuation; therefore, it is with infinite caution that I question them on this subject. A magnetic somnambulist is not always a physician; they can often be very good and very accurate in their prognoses for themselves, yet know nothing of how to judge them in others. Sometimes, after having possessed the ability to recognize illnesses, they may lose this ability, only to recover it at a certain time.

This observation is quite necessary to be pondered by those who must guide magnetic somnambulists. How many times, I am certain, it must have happened that they were dissatisfied with their answers, and saw many people put in rapport <term>Rapport: a technical term in magnetism referring to the specific energetic connection established between a magnetizer and a subject, or between a subject and another person being diagnosed.</term> with them leave feeling unsatisfied with their consultation! From this, there always follow well-founded doubts regarding the very reality of the state of magnetic somnambulism. Alas! ...ment <note>original: "sement"; This is the conclusion of the word "heureusement" (happily) or "entièrement" (entirely) from the previous page.</note>; but this man had the duties of his new position to fulfill; he was tormented by the anxiety of losing it if he stayed at my home too long; all these reasons determined me not to hold him any longer, especially as he had assured me, in the *magnetic state* <note>The "magnetic state" refers to the trance-like condition induced by the practitioner.</note>, that with the help of the regimen he had prescribed for himself, his health would be completely strengthened in the course of the winter.

I could acquire a certain well-being that I lack. It is with me (I am reporting his own expressions) as with a man with a modest fortune who feels the possibility of increasing it. I could never become as robust as a man of a better constitution than mine; but after all, there are relative perfections; and until I have acquired that of which I am capable, you will always be able to put me into a crisis <note>Crisis: the transformative physical or mental reaction during magnetic treatment which practitioners believed led to healing.</note>."

(18) Page 411. *Count Louis de Rieux*, in indicating lottery numbers while in the <term>magnetic state</term> <note>A trance-like state induced by animal magnetism, also known as mesmerism.</note>, did nothing, as has been noted, but yield to the insistence of *his father*; no specific insight guided his choice. The act of kindness he performed on this occasion was just as simple as the one he repeated in his natural state when he suggested five other numbers different from the first. It is well understood that the subsequent drawing did not fulfill any of his predictions.

I insist on this fact with all the more pleasure because it may serve as proof of what I have already repeated many times: that outside the sphere of the specific sensations of magnetic beings and those of the people with whom they are in <term>rapport</term> <note>The special psychological and physical connection between a magnetizer and their patient, allowing for shared sensations or thought transmission.</note>, there is no foundation to be found in any of the answers that indiscreet questions may suggest to them. I have had patients who, in the state of <term>magnetic somnambulism</term> <note>A term used to describe a state where a patient appears to be in a sleep-like trance but can speak, move, and perceive things beyond their normal senses.</note>, were sensitive enough to respond to my mere thought: *Victor*, *Joly*, *Vielet*, *Catherine Vidron*, etc., were of this number. Had I wished to deceive anyone by their means, and revive the ancient errors of the <term>oracles</term> <note>Divinely inspired prophets of the ancient world.</note> and the <term>sibyls</term> <note>Women in ancient times believed to utter the oracles and prophecies of a god.</note>, nothing would have been easier for me. From then on, without even speaking to them, I could have dictated their answers (with a wand in hand, had I wished to better fix my will and use it as a conductor), and passed them off as new <term>pythonists</term> <note>Fortune-tellers or oracular figures, named after the Pythia of Delphi.</note>; whereas, in all of that, I would have committed nothing more than a simple abuse of my physical power, forcing my patients into an act of compliance. They would have resisted this all the less because they were simple and placed their trust in me.

In this way, I understand very well how a highly enthusiastic <term>magnetizer</term> <note>A practitioner of animal magnetism, or Mesmerism, who believed they could heal others by directing a "vital fluid" through their will and touch.</note> could believe that a <term>magnetic somnambulist</term> <note>A patient in a trance-like state who appears asleep but is capable of responding to the magnetizer.</note> had seen men and ships on the moon, while they had only seen the wild ideas that the magnetizer had in his own head.

Self-knowledge and the study of our sensations—this is where the discovery of <term>magnetic somnambulism</term> can lead us, and the goal toward which we must strive, alongside that of relieving suffering humanity. This task is difficult to fulfill; but to obtain certain results, it is necessary, I repeat, that the primary desire of the magnetizer always be to heal their patient, and that the first knowledge of a magnetic being be that of their illness and the means to be employed to advance their recovery, of which, consequently, they must know the end. I confess that, without this primary data, it is impossible for me to place any confidence in all the claims of magnetic somnambulists.

...be indifferent to being cared for by a doctor and a nurse <note>Original: "garde." In this period, this refers to a bedside attendant or nurse, often a domestic or religious sister, rather than a modern registered nurse.</note> who hold affection for us.

Several cavalry officers have told me a fact that struck me because of the analogy I found between it and all my observations. When, within a <term>regiment</term>, one sees a horse wasting away without any apparent cause of illness, it is customary to change its rider. One man, through the affection he bears for his horse, maintains its vigor and health through his <term>grooming</term> <note>Original: "pansement." While this can mean a medical dressing, in a cavalry context, it refers to the daily care, cleaning, and tending of a horse.</note>; whereas in the hands of another, the same horse would have fallen into emaciation and decline. If this fact is true—as I have no reason to doubt—we must necessarily conclude that the affection of the beings who habitually surround us becomes just as vital to our health as to our happiness.

## ***POSTSCRIPT***

Since December 8, 1785—the day Dupré had left Buzancy <note>Buzancy is a commune in northern France where the Marquis de Puységur conducted his landmark experiments in "Animal Magnetism," famously using a "magnetized tree" to treat local peasants.</note>—I had not received any news from him. Being unable to doubt his punctuality in coming to find me, I had made no move to contact him, and I expected him with confidence by the end of the month of February. However, on the 12th of that same month, I received a letter from him, in which he informed me that it would be impossible for him to travel to Paris at the time I had set for him. I immediately wrote to the parish priest of his village at Bolhard, near Rouen, as well as to the Chevalier de Boniface, to whom he had appealed <note>Original: "dont il se réclamait." This suggests Dupré used the Chevalier as a character reference or patron.</note>, to urge them, by the most compelling reasons, to send Dupré to me as soon as possible. These gentlemen responded so well to my urgings that on Monday, February 20, Dupré arrived in Paris. Upon the first questions I asked him regarding his health, he replied that he had suffered a great deal since he had left me; that he had had a fever the previous month, as a result of which there remained some blisters
